title: Distributed Rate Limiting
description: Tackle the hard problems of rate limiting at scale — Redis Lua scripts for atomicity, race conditions, sliding window logs, and multi-region coordination.

segments.text: Rate limiting on a single server is straightforward. But when your API runs on fifty servers behind a load balancer, how do you enforce a global limit? If each server tracks its own count, a user can get fifty times the intended rate. Let's solve distributed rate limiting.

The core solution is a centralized counter in Redis. Every API server checks Redis before serving a request. Increment the counter, check the limit, allow or deny. Redis is perfect because it's fast, in-memory, and supports atomic operations.

But there's a race condition. Two requests arrive simultaneously on different servers. Both read the counter as 99 with a limit of 100. Both increment to 100 and allow the request. Now you've allowed 101 requests. This check-then-act is not atomic.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you make the read-check-increment operation atomic in Redis?

segments.text: Redis Lua scripts solve this elegantly. A Lua script executes atomically on the Redis server — no other command can interleave. Your script increments the counter and checks the limit in a single atomic operation. No race condition possible.

Fixed window rate limiting has an edge case. If the limit is 100 per minute and a user sends 100 requests at 11:59:59, then 100 more at 12:00:01, they've sent 200 requests in 2 seconds while technically staying within the per-minute limit.

Sliding window log fixes this. Store the timestamp of every request in a sorted set. To check the limit, count entries within the last 60 seconds from right now. Remove entries older than 60 seconds. The window slides continuously — no boundary exploits.

Sliding window log is accurate but memory-intensive — storing every timestamp for high-traffic users adds up. The sliding window counter is a compromise: it uses weighted counts from the current and previous fixed windows to approximate a sliding window. Less memory, nearly as accurate.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose the exact sliding log over the approximate sliding counter?

segments.text: Multi-region rate limiting is the hardest problem. If your API runs in US, Europe, and Asia, synchronizing counters across regions adds latency. You can use local counters with periodic sync, accepting some over-limit requests during the sync window.

A practical approach: give each region a portion of the global limit. If the global limit is 1000 per minute across 3 regions, give each region 333. If one region is underused, redistribute its quota. This avoids cross-region calls for every request.

Always communicate rate limit status to clients. Return headers like X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and Retry-After. Good clients will back off when they see limits approaching. Use HTTP 429 status for rate-limited requests.

Distributed rate limiting combines atomic counters, careful algorithm choice, and multi-region coordination. Redis Lua scripts give you atomicity, sliding windows prevent boundary exploits, and quota distribution handles global scale. It's a small feature with deep engineering.
